mainTopic: How רבי יהודה divides the dead ox without a תם paying more than a מועד, and a new משנה on an owner's liability for his ox versus himself
overview: The amud opens by finishing a challenge to רבא's reading of רבי יהודה: on that reading, a תם would come out stricter than a מועד. A משנה about guarding is offered as support, but the גמרא rejects it, because guarding (שמירה) is not payment (תשלומין). A ברייתא then shows, through a קל וחומר, that on payment רבי יהודה never lets a תם pay more than a מועד. So רבי יוחנן gives a new explanation: רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about who gets the carcass's increase in value, and רבי יהודה lets the מזיק share in it. Even so, a מזיק may never profit, and the פסוק ״שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם״ covers even the case where the ניזק loses nothing. Next, רב אחא בר תחליפא asks whether a תם would then pay more than half. The answer is that only the loss caused by the death is split, which the extra word ״וְגַם״ teaches. A new משנה then lists cases where an owner is liable for his ox's act but not his own, or the reverse. The death-penalty cases are among them. The גמרא discusses destructive acts on שבת and begins a challenge to רבי יוחנן from the haystack case, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The problem: a תם would end up stricter than a מועד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its challenge. On the reading of רבי יהודה just suggested, the owner of a תם would be treated more harshly than the owner of a מועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: That would mean a תם is stricter than a מועד!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a challenge that began just before this point. It shows that the reading of רבי יהודה being discussed leads to a strange result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a מועד, the dead ox belongs to the injured party, so any drop in its value is his loss alone. On the suggested reading of רבי יהודה, the owner of a תם would also share in that loss. That makes the less dangerous ox (the תם) the harsher one, which seems backwards.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox not yet known as a gorer; its owner pays only half the damage
A 'warned' ox that has gored repeatedly; its owner pays full damage
Stricter, more severe

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the end of a question that started earlier. It is a challenge (קשיא), not a ruling.

phrases.english: An innocuous ox is stricter than a forewarned ox!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge from the previous amud (34a) against רבא's suggested reading of רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggested reading of רבי יהודה, that the owner of a תם shares in the drop in value of the dead ox.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A מועד should always be treated at least as strictly as a תם. A reading that makes the תם stricter must be wrong.

steps.title: Possible answer: רבי יהודה does hold a תם can be stricter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that we accept the strange result. It points to a משנה where רבי יהודה says a תם brings liability and a מועד does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: yes, that is so. As we learned in a משנה, רבי יהודה says: for a תם he is liable, and for a מועד he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible way out: maybe רבי יהודה really does hold that a תם can be stricter than a מועד. It brings a משנה as support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה (later, on daf 45b) deals with a guardian who did not guard an ox properly. There רבי יהודה makes the guardian liable for a תם but not for a מועד. If רבי יהודה says this there, the result in Step 1 might not bother him.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you would say', introducing a possible answer
'Indeed so', accepting the point
'As we learned in a משנה'

phrases.english: And if you would say: indeed so,
as we learned in a mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says:
for an innocuous ox he is liable, and for a forewarned ox he is exempt;
phrases.notes: This is the משנה on daf 45b about someone who guarded an ox badly and it went out and caused damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a defense against the challenge in Step 1 by accepting its result.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepting the challenge's result, backed by a source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A תם being stricter than a מועד is impossible, so the reading must be wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה does allow a תם to be stricter elsewhere, so the reading can stand.

steps.title: Pushing back: that משנה is about guarding, not payment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the answer. רבי יהודה made the תם stricter only on guarding, where פסוקים teach it. That says nothing about how much is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that you heard רבי יהודה say this about guarding, since פסוקים are written about it. About payment, did you ever hear him say it?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the answer from Step 2. That משנה is about a different subject, so it cannot prove anything here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stricter rule for a תם in the משנה is about the level of guarding required, and it is learned from the פסוקים. Our question is about payment (how the carcass and the loss are divided). Nothing shows רבי יהודה ever made a תם stricter on payment, so the challenge in Step 1 is back.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Say that you heard him...', you heard it only in that case
Guarding the animal
Verses of the תורה
Payment for damage

steps.whyThisMatters: A rule from one area of law cannot simply be moved to another area. Guarding and payment are treated as separate questions.

phrases.english: Say that you heard Rabbi Yehuda say this
regarding guarding, since verses are written about it;
regarding payment, did you hear him say it?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the support brought in Step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the משנה about guarding.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה is about guarding, which is learned from פסוקים. It does not apply to payment.

steps.title: A ברייתא: what if both owners split the living and the dead ox?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא of רבי יהודה to show his view on payment. He starts with a case: an ox worth 100 gores an ox worth 20, and the carcass is worth 4. Should each side take half of the living ox and half of the dead one?
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי יהודה says: one might think that if an ox worth a מנה gored an ox worth five סלעים, and the carcass is worth a סלע, then this one takes half the living and half the dead, and that one takes half the living and half the dead?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that on payment, רבי יהודה does not let a תם be stricter. This step lays out the case that רבי יהודה is about to reject.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each side took half of each ox, the injured party would get 50 plus 2, which is 52, for an ox that was worth only 20. רבי יהודה raises this idea only to reject it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But it was taught in a ברייתא', bringing a source
'One might think', an idea that will be rejected
100 זוז (dinars)
A coin worth 4 זוז
The carcass of the dead animal

steps.confusionAlert: The word יָכוֹל ('one might think') means this is NOT the הלכה. It is an idea that רבי יהודה is about to reject.

phrases.english: But it was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says:
One might think: an ox worth a maneh (100 dinars)
that gored an ox worth five sela,
and the carcass is worth a sela,

phrases.aramaic: זֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת,
phrases.english: this one takes half the living and half the dead,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת?
phrases.english: and that one takes half the living and half the dead?
phrases.notes: That gives the injured party 52 for an ox worth 20, which is far more than his loss.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After Step 3 rejected the proof from guarding, this brings a source about payment that backs the challenge in Step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה does not let a תם pay more than a מועד.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's קל וחומר: a תם cannot pay more than a מועד
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rejects the 'split both oxen' idea with a קל וחומר. The rules for a מועד exist to make it stricter. A מועד pays only the damage it did, so a תם surely cannot pay more.
steps.simpleTranslation: You must say: why is a מועד singled out, to be stricter or more lenient? You must say, to be stricter. Now if a מועד pays only what it damaged, then a תם, which is more lenient, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה finishes the ברייתא by rejecting the idea from Step 4. This proves that on payment, he never lets a תם come out stricter than a מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קל וחומר goes like this: a מועד is the stricter case, yet it pays only the actual damage. So a תם, the lighter case, cannot pay more than the damage. This brings back the challenge from Step 1 against the suggested reading of רבי יהודה, now with a source about payment.

keyTerms.meaning: To make stricter
To make more lenient
'You must say', the only possible answer
'All the more so', the ending of a קל וחומר

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי יהודה, a תם never pays more than a מועד. Any reading of his view that makes the תם stricter on payment runs into this קל וחומר.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is the main source for the rule that a תם cannot pay more than a מועד. The rest of the sugya has to work with it.

phrases.english: You must say: why is a forewarned ox singled out?
To be stricter with it or to be more lenient with it?
You must say: to be stricter with it;
and if a forewarned ox pays only
what it damaged,
an innocuous ox, which is more lenient, all the more so?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא begun in Step 4 by rejecting its 'one might think' idea.
steps.raayaObject: On payment, רבי יהודה holds that a תם can never be stricter than a מועד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהודה's קל וחומר from the ברייתא
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The challenge of Step 1 is back in force: on payment, רבי יהודה does not let a תם come out stricter than a מועד.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: The argument is about the carcass going up in value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the earlier explanation. It says the real difference between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה is who gets the increase in the carcass's value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי יוחנן said: the difference between them is the increase in the carcass's value. One master holds it belongs to the ניזק, and the other holds it is split in half.
steps.whatsHappening: The earlier explanation led to a strange result and was rejected. So the גמרא brings a new explanation from רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is that the two תנאים do not argue about the carcass losing value. They argue about the carcass gaining value. רבי מאיר gives all the gain to the ניזק. רבי יהודה splits it, so the מזיק gets a share too.

keyTerms.meaning: The carcass going up in value after the ox died
There is a difference between them (the practical point they argue about)
The injured party, whose ox was killed
Half

steps.whyThisMatters: This explanation avoids the problem from the earlier steps. Under רבי יהודה, the owner of a תם would no longer pay more than the owner of a מועד.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Yochanan said:
The increase in the carcass's value is the difference between them,
for one master holds: it belongs to the injured party,
phrases.notes: This first master is רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: and one master holds: it is split in half.
phrases.notes: This second master is רבי יהודה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the explanation that was knocked down in steps 1-5 with a new one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining what the two sides argue about
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The argument was about the carcass losing value, which made a תם stricter than a מועד for רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is about the carcass gaining value. רבי יהודה lets the מזיק share in that gain.

steps.title: Why רבי יהודה worried: a case where the damager would profit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רבי יוחנן's view fits the worry in רבי יהודה's ברייתא. If the מזיק shares in the carcass's value, he could end up with more than his own ox was worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what bothered רבי יהודה: Now that you say the תורה has pity on the מזיק and lets him share in the increase, could it be that an ox worth five סלעים gores an ox worth a מנה, the carcass is worth fifty זוז, and each side takes half the living ox and half the dead one?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רבי יוחנן. The question in רבי יהודה's ברייתא makes sense only if רבי יהודה lets the מזיק share in the carcass.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Five סלעים equals 20 זוז, and a מנה equals 100 זוז. If they split both oxen, the מזיק gets 10 from the living ox and 25 from the carcass, which is 35. That is more than his ox was worth. The ברייתא's worry about this proves that, for רבי יהודה, the מזיק normally does share in the carcass's gain.

keyTerms.meaning: The תורה (literally "the Merciful One") has pity
The one who caused the damage (here, the owner of the goring ox)
A coin worth 4 זוז
100 זוז
A basic coin (the same as a דינר)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the case from step 4. There, a strong ox (100) killed a weak ox (20), and the worry was the ניזק getting too much. Here a weak ox (20) kills a strong ox (100), and רבי יהודה's worry is the מזיק making a profit.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַיְינוּ דְּקָא קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה –
phrases.english: And this is what was difficult for Rabbi Yehuda:
Now that you say
the Torah has pity on the damager,
in that he takes a share of the increase;
could it be that an ox worth five sela
that gored an ox worth a maneh (100 zuz),
and the carcass is worth fifty zuz –

phrases.aramaic: זֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת,
phrases.english: this one takes half the living ox and half the dead one,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת?
phrases.english: and that one takes half the living ox and half the dead one?
phrases.notes: Do the math: the מזיק would get 10 + 25 = 35, more than his 20-זוז ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּקָא קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יוחנן's explanation from step 6 by showing that it fits the worry in רבי יהודה's ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה lets the מזיק share in the carcass's increase in value
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהודה's ברייתא, which worries about the מזיק getting more than his ox was worth

steps.title: A damager never profits, and the פסוק says the owner only pays
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rejects splitting both oxen in that case. He gives two reasons: a מזיק never makes a profit, and the פסוק ״שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם״ teaches that the owner pays and does not collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: You must say: where do we ever find a מזיק making a profit, that this one should profit? And the פסוק also says ״שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם״: the owner pays, and the owner does not take.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה answers his own question. The מזיק cannot come out ahead, first because of logic and second because of a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason is logical: nowhere in the תורה does a person who causes damage come out with a gain. The second reason comes from the פסוק: the owner of the goring ox is described as one who pays, not as one who collects. So the מזיק can share in the carcass's gain, but never past the point of making a profit.

keyTerms.meaning: Comes out ahead / makes a profit
"He shall surely pay" (שמות 21:36)
"And it says": brings an extra proof, usually from a פסוק

phrases.english: You must say: where do we find a damager profiting,
that this one should profit?
And it says: "He shall surely pay" –
the owner pays,
and the owner does not take.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יהודה's answer to the question raised in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That the מזיק's share in the carcass's gain is capped so that he never profits
steps.raayaSupportSource: A logical rule (a מזיק never profits) and the פסוק ״שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם״

steps.title: Why was the פסוק needed on top of the logic?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה added ״וְאוֹמֵר״ and a פסוק, when the logical rule seemed to be enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of "and it says"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short clarifying question. It wants to know what the extra פסוק teaches beyond the logic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If "a מזיק never profits" already settles the case, the פסוק looks extra. The גמרא assumes the פסוק must cover some case that the logic does not.

keyTerms.meaning: What? (here: what is the purpose of)

phrases.english: What is the point of "and it says"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the second proof in step 8 was needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the פסוק adds beyond the logical rule that a מזיק never profits

steps.title: A case where the ניזק loses nothing: does the damager still share the gain?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to answer. Someone might think the 'no profit' logic only applies when the ניזק loses money. When the ניזק loses nothing, maybe the מזיק could share the gain and come out ahead.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: this rule applies only where the ניזק suffers a loss. But where the ניזק suffers no loss, for example an ox worth five סלעים gores an ox worth five סלעים and the carcass is worth thirty זוז, the מזיק also takes a share of the increase.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its answer by describing a mistaken idea the פסוק comes to rule out. Step 11 completes the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both oxen are worth 20 זוז and the carcass rose to 30. If they split, each side gets 10 + 15 = 25, so the ניזק ends up with more than his ox was worth. Since the ניזק lost nothing, the logical rule might not seem to apply, which would let the מזיק profit. The פסוק is needed to rule that out.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (introduces a mistaken idea to be ruled out)
This rule applies (only in this case)
A loss

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the גמרא's final ruling. It is a mistaken idea that the פסוק comes to reject, and step 11 gives that rejection.

phrases.english: And if you would say: this rule applies
where there is a loss to the injured party;
but where there is no loss to the injured party –
for example, an ox worth five sela
that gored an ox worth five sela,
and the carcass is worth thirty zuz –
phrases.notes: That is more than the 20 זוז the ox was worth alive, so the carcass went up in value.

phrases.english: the damager also takes a share of the increase;

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא פְּסֵידָא לְנִיזָּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the question in step 9 by describing a case the logical rule alone might not cover.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק covers a case where the ניזק loses nothing. There, the logical rule alone might seem to let the מזיק share the gain and profit (step 11 completes the answer).

steps.title: The פסוק shows the damager never gains
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its answer. The פסוק ״שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם״ is needed even when the ניזק loses nothing, to teach that the owner who caused damage pays and never comes out ahead.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why רבי יהודה added: "And it says: 'He shall surely pay.'" This teaches that the owner pays, and the owner does not take.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the answer it began in Step 10. רבי יהודה needed the פסוק for the case where logic alone might let the מזיק share in a gain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic "a מזיק never profits" might only apply when the ניזק is losing money. The פסוק covers every case: the owner who caused the damage is the one who pays, never the one who collects. So even when the ניזק loses nothing, the מזיק cannot end up with more than his ox was worth.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall surely pay (the פסוק about damages)
The owner (here, of the ox that did the damage)
Take, collect

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה uses two tools: logic (a מזיק never profits) and a פסוק (the owner pays and does not take). The פסוק covers the case the logic might not reach.

phrases.english: And it says: "He shall surely pay"
the owner pays,
and the owner does not take.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun in Step 10 to the question of Step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יהודה needed a פסוק in addition to logic.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק teaches that the owner who caused damage never collects, even in a case where the ניזק loses nothing and the logic might not apply.

steps.title: Would a תם end up paying more than half?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר תחליפא challenges רבא. If רבי יהודה splits both the live ox and the dead ox, a תם would sometimes pay more than half the damage, but the תורה says a תם pays only half.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר תחליפא said to רבא: If so, according to רבי יהודה a תם sometimes pays more than half the damage. But the תורה said: "They shall sell the live ox and divide its money"!
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge opens. רב אחא בר תחליפא says that splitting both oxen would make a תם pay more than half damage in some cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה limits a תם to paying half the damage, which is learned from splitting the live ox. If each side takes half of both oxen, the owner of the goring ox could lose more than half of the actual damage. That would break the תורה's half-damage limit.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox that has not yet gored three times; its owner pays only half the damage
Half the damage
And they shall divide its money
If so

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an attack on the 'no profit' rule. It is a different worry: the other side, where the מזיק might lose too much.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר תַּחְלִיפָא לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Tachlifa said to Rava:
If so, we find according to Rabbi Yehuda
a tam pays more than half the damage,
but the Torah said:
"They shall sell the live ox
and divide its money"!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר תַּחְלִיפָא לְרָבָא: אִם כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against רבי יהודה's method of splitting both oxen.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's ruling that each side takes half the live ox and half the dead ox.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Splitting both oxen can make the owner of a תם lose more than half the damage, which goes against the Torah's half-damage rule.

steps.title: Only the loss from the death is split
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that רבי יהודה also holds that only the drop in value caused by the death is split using the live ox. So the תם never pays more than half.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה holds: the loss that the death caused is split using the live ox.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge. רבי יהודה agrees that the תם pays only half of the loss caused by the death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer adds a limit to רבי יהודה's view. Whatever the split looks like, the payment is capped at half the drop in value from the death. This keeps the Torah's half-damage rule in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Drop in value, loss
Death
They split
He holds

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda holds:
the loss that the death caused
is split using the live ox.
phrases.notes: He means the תם's owner only covers half of the value the dead ox lost by dying, never more.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the opinion: רבי יהודה also holds a cap on payment.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Splitting both oxen could make a תם pay more than half damage.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה agrees that the payment is limited to half of the loss caused by the death.

steps.title: Where does רבי יהודה learn this limit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for רבי יהודה's source. It cannot be ״וְגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן״, because he already used that פסוק to teach that each side takes half of both oxen.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where does he learn this from? From "And the dead one too they shall divide"? But רבי יהודה already used that פסוק to teach that this one takes half the live and half the dead, and that one takes half the live and half the dead!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי יהודה gets the rule from Step 13. It points out that the obvious פסוק is already being used for something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר learns the 'loss from death' rule from ״וְגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן״. But רבי יהודה reads that same פסוק as the source for splitting both oxen. One פסוק usually cannot be used for two separate lessons, so the source of רבי יהודה's limit is in question.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he know this?
And the dead one too they shall divide
He took it out (he used the פסוק for another lesson)

phrases.english: From where does he know this?
From "And the dead one too they shall divide"?!
But didn't Rabbi Yehuda already use it

phrases.aramaic: לְזֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת,
phrases.english: for: this one takes half the live and half the dead,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת!
phrases.english: and that one takes half the live and half the dead!

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָא לֵיהּ? מִ״וְּגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 13 by asking for its source.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 13 that רבי יהודה holds the 'loss from death' rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק that teaches this rule (״וְגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן״) is already used by רבי יהודה for splitting both oxen, so it cannot also be his source here.

steps.title: The extra word 'also' teaches two things
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the word ״וְגַם״ is extra. So the פסוק teaches two rules: the dead ox is divided, and a תם never pays more than half.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the פסוק only meant to teach that the dead ox is divided, it could have said just 'and the dead one.' Why does it say 'also'? Learn two things from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 14. The same פסוק can be the source for both of רבי יהודה's rules, because the word ״וְגַם״ is extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 asked how one פסוק could teach two rules. The answer is that ״וְאֶת הַמֵּת״ alone would teach that the dead ox is divided. The extra word ״וְגַם״ adds a second lesson: only the drop in value is split, so the תם never pays more than half.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And also.' Here it is an extra word that teaches an extra rule.
'Learn two things from it.' One פסוק is teaching two rules.
'If so.' The גמרא is showing what the פסוק would have said if it only meant one thing.

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי יהודה, ״וְגַם אֶת הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן״ teaches two rules: both sides share the dead ox, and a תם never pays more than half the damage.

phrases.english: If so, let the verse write: 'and the dead one'!
phrases.notes: If the פסוק only meant 'divide the dead ox,' these words alone would have been enough. שמות 21:35

phrases.english: What is 'also' for?
Learn two things from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 14, which asked how one פסוק could serve as the source for two rules.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra word in the פסוק (ריבוי): the extra word supplies the second rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק was thought to be already used up for teaching that the dead ox is divided.
steps.terutzMaskana: ״וְאֶת הַמֵּת״ teaches the dividing, and the extra ״וְגַם״ teaches that a תם never pays more than half.

steps.title: New משנה: ox's act versus the owner's own act
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states a general rule. Sometimes an owner is liable for his ox's act but exempt for his own act, and sometimes the reverse.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Sometimes a person is liable for what his ox did but exempt for doing the same thing himself. And sometimes he is exempt for what his ox did but liable for doing it himself.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a general headline. It is setting up the examples that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we would expect a person to be held at least as responsible for his own act as for his ox's act. The משנה says this is not always true. The rules for an ox's damage and for a person's own act can come out differently in both directions.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה.' A new משנה starts here.
The act of his ox.
His own act.
Liable (must pay) / exempt (does not pay).

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
There is one who is liable for the act of his ox
but exempt for his own act,
and one who is exempt for the act of his ox
but liable for his own act.

steps.triggerLanguage: יֵשׁ חַיָּיב עַל מַעֲשֵׂה שׁוֹרוֹ וּפָטוּר עַל מַעֲשֵׂה עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה. It is not connected to the רבי יהודה discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An owner's liability for his ox's act can differ from his liability for his own act, in either direction.

steps.title: Exempt for the ox, liable for himself: shame and the slave
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives examples where the owner is exempt for his ox but liable for himself: shaming someone, and blinding or knocking out the tooth of his own slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? If his ox shamed someone, he is exempt. If he shamed someone himself, he is liable. If his ox blinded his slave's eye or knocked out his tooth, he is exempt. If he did it himself, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts filling in examples, beginning with the second half of its headline: exempt for the ox, liable for himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two examples here. Paying for shame applies when the person himself shamed someone, not when his ox did. If a master himself blinds his slave's eye or knocks out his tooth, he must free the slave. If his ox did it, he does not have to free him.

keyTerms.meaning: 'How so?' The משנה is about to give examples.
Shamed or embarrassed someone (בֹּשֶׁת).
Blinded his eye.
Knocked out his tooth.

steps.confusionAlert: The headline listed 'liable for the ox, exempt for himself' first. The examples start with the opposite case: 'exempt for the ox, liable for himself.'

phrases.english: How so?
If his ox shamed someone, he is exempt,
but if he himself shamed someone, he is liable.
If his ox blinded his slave's eye
or knocked out his tooth, he is exempt,
phrases.notes: For the slave, 'liable' means the master must set him free. שמות 21:26–27

phrases.english: but if he himself blinded his slave's eye
or knocked out his tooth, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives examples for the second half of the headline in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner is exempt if his ox shamed someone or blinded or broke the tooth of his slave, but liable if he did these himself.

steps.title: Liable for the ox, exempt for himself: parents and שבת
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives examples where the owner is liable for his ox but exempt for himself: injuring his own parent, and burning a haystack on שבת. He is exempt because doing these himself makes him liable to death.
steps.simpleTranslation: If his ox injured his father or mother, he is liable. If he injured them himself, he is exempt. If his ox set fire to a haystack on שבת, he is liable. If he set fire to it himself on שבת, he is exempt, because he is liable with his life.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the examples for the first half of its headline: liable for the ox, exempt for himself. It ends with the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When his ox does the damage, there is no death penalty, so the owner pays normally. When he himself injures a parent or burns on שבת, he is liable to death. A person who is liable to death does not also pay money for the same act.

keyTerms.meaning: Injured or wounded someone.
A stack of grain or hay.
He is liable with his life, meaning he gets the death penalty.

steps.whatToRemember: A person who is liable to death for an act does not pay money for that act. That is why he is exempt when he himself injures a parent or burns on שבת, but liable when his ox does it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rule that a death penalty and a money payment for the same act do not go together. The גמרא will build on this.

phrases.english: If his ox injured his father or his mother, he is liable,
but if he himself injured his father or mother, he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹרוֹ שֶׁהִדְלִיק אֶת הַגָּדִישׁ בְּשַׁבָּת – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: If his ox set fire to a haystack on Shabbat, he is liable,

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא שֶׁהִדְלִיק אֶת הַגָּדִישׁ בְּשַׁבָּת – פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: but if he himself set fire to the haystack on Shabbat, he is exempt,
because he is liable with his life.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives examples for the first half of the headline in step 16 and adds the reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner is liable when his ox injures his parent or burns a haystack on שבת. He is exempt when he does these himself, because he is liable to death.

steps.title: A teaching: destructive acts on שבת are exempt, except injuring and kindling
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו recites a ברייתא before רבי יוחנן. Anyone who does a מלאכה in a destructive way on שבת is exempt, except one who injures and one who kindles.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו taught before רבי יוחנן: All who do work destructively on שבת are exempt, except for one who injures and one who kindles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא on our משנה begins by quoting a ברייתא. It says destroying is not a punishable מלאכה on שבת, with two exceptions: injuring and kindling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a מלאכה on שבת must build or accomplish something to be punishable. This ברייתא says injuring and kindling are punishable even when done only to destroy. This matters for our משנה, which said a person who burns a haystack on שבת is exempt from paying because he deserves death.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who does a מלאכה in a destructive way, not building or fixing anything
One who injures another person
One who kindles a fire
Taught / recited (a ברייתא)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'exempt' (פטורין) means exempt from punishment for breaking שבת. It does not refer to paying damages.

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: תָּנֵי רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu taught before Rabbi Yochanan:
All who act destructively are exempt,
except for one who injures and one who kindles.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה's case of burning a haystack on שבת (step 18).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Destructive מלאכה on שבת is exempt, except injuring and kindling, which are punishable even when destructive.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן rejects the teaching
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן tells רבי אבהו to take this ברייתא outside. The exception for injuring and kindling is not an accepted teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Go out and teach it outside! Injuring and kindling is not a reliable משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן strongly rejects the ברייתא. He says its exception for injuring and kindling should not be relied on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יוחנן, injuring and kindling follow the same rule as every other מלאכה. If they are done destructively, the person is exempt. The ברייתא is treated as not authoritative.

keyTerms.meaning: Go out and teach it outside, meaning it does not belong in the בית מדרש
It is not an accepted teaching

phrases.english: He said to him: Go out and teach it outside!
phrases.notes: רבי יוחנן means this teaching is not good enough to learn in the בית מדרש.

phrases.english: Injuring and kindling is not a mishna.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the ברייתא quoted in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The exception for injuring and kindling in the ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ruling is not authoritative. Destructive injuring and kindling should be exempt like every other destructive act.

steps.title: If accepted, it applies only when there is a useful purpose
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן adds that even if the ברייתא is accepted, it is talking about cases with a purpose. The injurer needs the blood for his dog, and the kindler needs the ashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you insist that it is a reliable teaching: the injurer is liable only where he needs the blood for his dog, and the kindler only where he needs the ashes.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן offers a second way out. He explains the ברייתא so that it fits the general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In these cases the act is not purely destructive, because something useful comes out of it. So the general rule stays the same: a purely destructive act is exempt, and injuring and kindling are not real exceptions.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you insist on saying
Needs it for his dog (the blood, as food)
Its ashes

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, injuring and kindling on שבת are punishable only when they have a constructive purpose, like blood for the dog or ashes for use.

phrases.english: And if you insist on saying it is a mishna:
one who injures, where he needs it for his dog,
phrases.notes: The word 'blood' is left out but assumed: he wants the blood to feed his dog.

phrases.english: one who kindles, where he needs its ashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fallback to step 20: instead of rejecting the ברייתא, it limits it to useful cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא) to a constructive purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seems to say injuring and kindling are punishable even when purely destructive.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא refers only to cases with some benefit, so the rule that destructive acts are exempt stays in place.

steps.title: Setting up a challenge from the משנה's haystack case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes our משנה: if one's ox burns a haystack on שבת, the owner pays, but if he burns it himself, he is exempt. The person's case is compared to his ox's, and an ox has no use for the ashes. The challenge continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: if his ox set fire to a haystack on שבת, he is liable, and if he set fire to a haystack on שבת, he is exempt. The משנה teaches his case as similar to his ox's case. Just as with his ox, it does not need the ashes...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge to רבי יוחנן from our own משנה. The argument is not finished here; it continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the person is exempt from paying because burning the haystack makes him liable to death (step 18). The גמרא points out that his case is described like the ox's case, and an ox does not want the ashes. That suggests the person also did not need the ashes, so his kindling was purely destructive, yet it still seems to be a punishable act on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned (in a משנה)
A haystack (a stack of grain)
Similar to / parallel to
Does not need it

steps.confusionAlert: The question is cut off in the middle. Do not look for the conclusion yet; it comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: We learned in the mishna:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹרוֹ שֶׁהִדְלִיק אֶת הַגָּדִישׁ בְּשַׁבָּת – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: If his ox set fire to a haystack on Shabbat, he is liable,
phrases.notes: This is the case from our משנה that we saw in step 18.

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא שֶׁהִדְלִיק אֶת הַגָּדִישׁ בְּשַׁבָּת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: but if he set fire to a haystack on Shabbat, he is exempt.
And it teaches his case as similar to his ox's case:
just as with his ox, it does not need it,
phrases.notes: 'It' means the ashes. An ox has no use for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: שׁוֹרוֹ שֶׁהִדְלִיק אֶת הַגָּדִישׁ בְּשַׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's position from steps 20–21 using the משנה's haystack case from step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's view that destructive kindling (without needing the ashes) is not punishable on שבת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה describes the person's act like the ox's act, and the ox does not need the ashes. So the person's kindling seems purely destructive, yet the משנה treats it as deserving death.
